---
title: "Diseases: states, transitions, and rates"
jupyter: python3
---

A disease in Starsim is declared the way a compartmental model is drawn: as the states people can be in (the compartments) and the transitions between them (the flows), each with what drives it, a rate or a duration. This page is the reference for writing them: the ways to write a transition, transmission and other rates, durations and their distributions, branching, how an epidemic starts, births and deaths, quantities that are not people, and susceptibility. A disease declared this way runs as a compartmental model or as agents, unchanged.

For a step-by-step introduction, see [Building your model](../tutorials/t2_model.qmd) and [Disease structure](../tutorials/t3_structure.qmd). A disease that needs more than states and transitions can be written as code; see [Modules written as code](models_code.qmd).

## A disease in brief

The simplified measles model used throughout these pages is an SIR model:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the share infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.equations()
```

`ss.states()` makes the states, named in one string. A transition is written `source >> destination @ driver`: "S goes to I at 1.9 times I". What follows `@` is one of:

- a **rate**, per person in the source state per unit of time, such as `ss.perday(0.125)`, or an expression of states and parameters, such as `1.9*I`;
- a **duration**, such as `ss.days(8)`: the average time people spend in the source state before they take this transition. A duration of 8 days and a rate of 1/8 per day are the same transition.

A bare number in a rate takes the model's unit of time, here days, from `ss.days(8)`; see [Parameters](models_parameters.qmd#units-of-time). Names come from the variables: the states are `S`, `I`, and `R`, the transitions `infection` and `recovery`, and the disease `measles`, and so are their results (`sim.results.measles.infection`).

## Ways to write a transition

There is one kind of transition, `ss.Transition`, and the operators are a short way to write it. These build the same model:

```{python}
# Operators: the usual form
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)

# Named by keyword, e.g. when the transitions are written inline
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    init_prev = 0.001,
)

# Fully explicit, e.g. to build a model in a loop, or from R
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=1.9*I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'measles',
)
```

A transition that has no variable or keyword to be named by gets a name from its states (`S_to_I`). A disease can also be written as a class, which is the form for a disease that goes into a library ([below](#the-class-form)).

## Transmission

### Frequency- and density-dependent transmission

A bare state in a rate, like `I` in `1.9*I`, means contact with the people in that state. With no contacts given (homogeneous mixing), that is the share of the population in it, `I/N`, so `S >> I @ beta*I` is the textbook frequency-dependent transmission, with a flow of β S I / N. With a contact matrix or a network, the same rate is worked out from whom each person actually meets, and β is the rate per contact (see [Stratification](models_stratification.qmd) and [Contact matrices](populations_contacts.qmd)). A transition whose rate contains a bare state is **contact-mediated**, and that state is a source of infection.

For density-dependent transmission, in which the number of contacts grows with the size of the population (as is often assumed for animal or vector populations), write the count itself, `I.n`. The flow is then β S I:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles_density = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9e-5*I.n, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)
measles_density.equations()
```

A rate can also be written as the whole flow, as in the equations of other frameworks: `S >> I @ beta*S*I/N` (with `N = S + I + R`) is the same frequency-dependent model as `beta*I`, and `beta*S*I` the same density-dependent model as `beta*I.n`.

### Several sources of infection

Several sources are a sum: `S >> E @ beta*(I + 0.5*A)` says that people in `A` (say, without symptoms) are half as infectious as those in `I`. A rate must be linear in its bare states, since exposure on a network is a sum over contacts; anything nonlinear is written with counts (`I.n`).

## Other rates

Anything that is not transmission is a rate per person, or a duration:

| After `@` | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| a duration | the mean time in the source state | `I >> R @ ss.days(8)` |
| a distribution of durations | the time in the source state, with that distribution | `I >> R @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(8))` |
| a rate, or a bare number | a rate per person per unit of time | `R >> S @ ss.peryear(0.1)`, `R >> S @ 0.1` |
| a probability per period | the chance of moving in each period, as a rate | `I >> R @ ss.prob(0.12, 'day')` |
| an expression with a bare state | transmission | `S >> I @ beta*I` |
| an expression of counts | a rate that depends on how many people are in each state | `S >> I @ beta*W.n/(W.n + K)` |
| a function of the sim | a rate worked out at each step | `S >> I @ my_rate` |

A bare number after `@` is always a rate, never a duration: `I >> R @ 8` means a rate of 8 per day, so that people stay infectious for an eighth of a day. A duration is always typed (`ss.days(8)`), or given as `dur=` (`ss.Transition(I, R, dur=8)`).

Transitions out of the same state that are driven by rates (or durations with an exponential distribution) compete: the total rate of leaving is their sum, and each takes its share of those who leave. The order in which they are written doesn't matter.

## Durations

A single duration is the mean of an exponential distribution, as in an ODE model, and `describe()` marks this as a guess. An exponential distribution has a lot of spread: with a mean of 10 days, a third of people leave within 4 days, and one in twenty stays more than 30. The real latent period of measles (from infection to becoming infectious) is about 10 days in nearly everyone. A distribution with less spread is given in its place:

```{python}
import numpy as np

def make_measles(latent):
    """ Measles with a latent period: S -> E -> I -> R """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    onset     = E >> I @ latent
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    return ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

latents = {
    'Exponential':      ss.days(10),
    'Erlang, 4 stages': ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10)),
    'Fixed':            ss.constant(ss.days(10)),
}
for label, latent in latents.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(latent), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    I = sim.results.measles.I
    print(label, '- peak infectious:', round(I.max()), 'on day', np.argmax(I.values))
```

All three have the same mean, and so the same R0, but with an exponential latent period some people become infectious within days, which brings the epidemic forward. The more realistic the distribution, the later and higher the peak.

The distributions most used for durations are:

| Distribution | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Exponential | The ODE default; a constant rate of leaving | `ss.days(10)` |
| Erlang (a gamma distribution with a whole number of stages, `k`) | A duration with less spread: the standard deviation is the mean divided by √k | `ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))` |
| Fixed | Everyone stays exactly this long, e.g. a reporting delay | `ss.constant(ss.days(10))` |
| Lognormal | A duration given by its mean and standard deviation, e.g. from a study | `ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2))` |

Any other distribution of durations works too; see [Distributions](models_distributions.qmd). As agents, each person draws their own time in the state. As compartments, an Erlang distribution is run exactly, as `k` stages in a row; a fixed duration is run exactly too (as one compartment for each step people have been in the state); and any other distribution is run as Erlang stages with the same mean and standard deviation, with a note that says so. `stages=k` on a transition (`ss.Transition(E, I, dur=ss.days(10), stages=4)`) says how many stages to use, under every solver.

## Branching

Some people go one way and some another: most people with measles recover, but a small share die. There are two ways to say this, and they differ in when the branch is decided.

**Separate transitions with `p=`** are decided when people enter the state, and each branch can have its own duration. Here 0.2% of people with measles die, and `ss.null` is outside the model:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.998)
death     = ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.002)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, death, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim.results.measles.death.sum()))
```

**One transition with several destinations**, given as a list with `p=` for the share going to each, is decided when people leave. Its result is the total, and each destination has a result of its own, `<transition>.<state>`. Here the dead are kept as a state, `D`, so that they can be counted:

```{python}
S, I, R, D = ss.states('S I R D')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
outcome   = ss.Transition(I, [R, D], p=[0.998, 0.002], dur=ss.days(8))
measles = ss.Disease(infection, outcome, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
print('Deaths:', round(res['outcome.D'].sum()))
print('Dead at the end:', round(res.D[-1]))
```

The shares out of one state must add up to 1; one of them can be left as `None`, for the rest. A share can vary by age group or in time, like any other value ([Parameters](models_parameters.qmd)).

## How the epidemic starts

Three options say who is in which state at the start, and everyone not placed elsewhere starts in the first state (`S`):

- `init_prev=` is the share of people who start infected (the initial prevalence). They start in the state that an infection leads to: `I` in an SIR model, but `E` in an SEIR model, where nobody is then infectious at the start (a note says so). A number above 1 is a number of people.
- `init=` is the share of people who start in each state, e.g. `init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9)` for an outbreak in a population that is 90% immune.
- `init_n=` is the number of people who start in each state, e.g. `init_n=dict(I=10)`.

If nothing is given, a disease with transmission starts with 1% of people infected (`init_prev=0.01`), which `describe()` marks as a guess. Values can also be given by group, with `ss.by()`; see [Stratification](models_stratification.qmd#values-by-group).

## Births and deaths in a disease

Births and deaths of everyone are usually given to the sim, as `demographics=`, so that the same people are born into and die from every disease ([Demographics](populations_demographics.qmd)). With one disease, they can also be declared in it: `ss.birth(S, rate=...)` is a crude birth rate into `S` (a typed rate is per person; a bare number is per year, and above 1 per 1,000 people), and `ss.death(rate=...)` with no state is a death rate in every state, read the same way. A death from one state, `ss.death(I, rate=...)`, is a rate like any other: a bare number is in the model's unit.

New births are the supply of susceptible people that keeps measles endemic. Here is measles in a city of a million, starting from a population in which it has circulated before, so that only 7% of people are still susceptible. Since this model has values in both days and years, the unit of a bare number can't be known, so β is given as `ss.perday()`:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    births    = ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), # 20 births per 1,000 people per year
    deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),    # The same death rate, so the population is stable
    init      = dict(S=0.07, I=0.0001),             # The rest start in R, immune
)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=1_000_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.days(1))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.resample('month').plot()
```

(The sim prints R0 = 15.2 and, since 93% start immune, R = 1.07 at the start; see [The reproduction number](models_building.qmd#the-reproduction-number).) Each epidemic uses up the susceptible people faster than births replace them, and then dies down until births have built them up again. So epidemics recur, here about every two years, and get smaller, towards a steady endemic level at which births balance infections. The period is close to the classical approximation 2π√(AD), with A ≈ 1/(μ(R0 − 1)) ≈ 3.6 years the mean age at infection (for a death rate μ of 0.02 per year) and D = 8 days the infectious period. In this deterministic model the epidemics damp out; [Parameters over time](models_parameters.qmd#parameters-over-time) shows how seasonal contacts keep them going. In a stochastic model the infection can also die out between epidemics in a small population; see [Solvers](running_solvers.qmd).

## States that are not people

Some of what a model tracks is not people: bacteria in water, or a population of mosquitoes. These are states too, declared with `people=False`. They are counts, not people: they are never agents, aren't counted in the population, and are used in rates as counts (`W.n`). Here is a cholera model with bacteria shed into the water by infectious people (after Codeço, 2001):

```{python}
beta = 0.5 # Rate of infection per day at a high concentration of bacteria
K    = 1e5 # Concentration of bacteria (cells/mL) that gives half that rate
xi   = 10  # Cells/mL shed per infectious person per day

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
W = ss.State(people=False) # Bacteria in the water: a count, not people
cholera = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * W.n/(W.n + K),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5),
    shedding  = ss.null >> W @ xi*I.n,    # An inflow: the total per day
    decay     = W >> ss.null @ ss.days(30), # The mean lifetime in the water
    init      = dict(I=0.001),
)
sim = ss.Sim(cholera, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', stop=365, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.cholera.plot()
```

Since nobody catches cholera from a person here, the infection is **spontaneous** (its rate has no bare state), but it is still the acquisition of the disease: it is what a vaccine or a lower susceptibility acts on.

A count can weight each person: `(ss.by(biting=[0.5, 1, 2])*I).n` counts each infectious person by how much they are bitten (in a model stratified by `biting`), and `I.n_trans` by how infectious they are (their `rel_trans`, with any product or modifier on it), so a treatment that halves infectiousness also halves what the treated shed: `shedding = ss.null >> W @ xi*I.n_trans`. A weighted count works under every solver, worked out once a step in a compartmental run.

## Susceptibility and infectiousness

A state can make the people in it less susceptible, or less infectious, than others, with `rel_sus` and `rel_trans`. For example, people vaccinated against measles (`V`) are 97% protected:

```{python}
def make_measles(coverage):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    V = ss.State(rel_sus=0.03) # Vaccinated: 3% as susceptible as others
    infection = S + V >> I @ 1.9*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(V=coverage, I=0.0001), name='measles')

for coverage in [0.85, 0.90, 0.95]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(coverage), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    print('Coverage', coverage, '- infections in a year:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
```

`S + V >> I` is one transition from either state. Even 95% coverage doesn't stop the outbreak: with R0 ≈ 15, the share of people who must be immune to stop spread (the herd immunity threshold, 1 − 1/R0) is 93%, and 95% coverage with a vaccine that is 97% effective protects 92%.

Each person also has their own `rel_sus` and `rel_trans`, which interventions and connectors change: a vaccine lowers the `rel_sus` of those who get it ([Products and deliveries](interventions_products.qmd)), and `ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, ...)` can make one disease change the risk of another ([Connectors](interventions_connectors.qmd)). These act on the transitions that are an **acquisition** of the disease: every transmission, and any other transition out of the first state if the disease has no transmission (as for cholera above). To say otherwise, give `acquisition=True` or `False` to the transition; `describe()` lists which transitions it took as acquisitions.

## The library's SIR, SIS, and SEIR

`ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, and `ss.SEIR` are declared diseases with named parameters: `beta`, `dur_inf`, `init_prev`, `p_death` (0 by default), and `dur_exp` for the SEIR. Their results are the same as any declared disease's, a result for each state and transition, plus a `prevalence` that each declares as a ratio of its states (`prevalence = I/(S + I + R)` in the SIR, `(E + I)/(S + E + I + R)` in the SEIR):

```{python}
sir = ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(1.9), dur_inf=ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print(sim.results.sir.keys())
```

## The class form

A disease can also be a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body. This is the form for a disease that goes into a library, or that is made many times with different values. Its parameters can then be given when it is made:

```{python}
class Measles(ss.Disease):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta      = ss.par(ss.perday(1.9), bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate', source='Gives R0 of about 15')
    infection = S >> E @ beta*I
    onset     = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

measles = Measles(beta=1.5, init=dict(I=0.001)) # Named "measles", after the class
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.plot()
```

A class can also have methods, for behavior that isn't a transition: override `step()`, and call `super().step()` to run the declared transitions ([Modules written as code](models_code.qmd)).

## Pitfalls

- **A bare number after `@` is a rate.** `I >> R @ 8` is a rate of 8 per day, not 8 days; write `ss.days(8)`.
- **A rate with no state in it is not transmission.** `S >> I @ 0.2` infects everyone in `S` at 0.2 per day whether or not anyone is infectious. Transmission names its source: `S >> I @ beta*I`.
- **`init_prev` in an SEIR model starts people in `E`.** To start some people infectious, give `init=dict(I=...)`.
